lead: A Yagi-Uda antenna gets a directional beam from one driven dipole and a row of rods that are not connected to anything. It is cheap and light and gives 7 to 15 dBi, but only over a few per cent of bandwidth. A log-periodic dipole array (LPDA) makes the opposite trade: every dipole is fed, the dipoles grow in a fixed ratio from front to back, and the antenna keeps its pattern over a 3:1 or 10:1 band. Yagis point at TV transmitters from rooftops across India; LPDAs serve EMC test labs, HF stations and wideband monitoring.
prereq: You need: two-element arrays for the one-sided cardioid pair, uniform linear arrays for end-fire, and the half-wave and folded dipoles from the antenna fundamentals topic.

blocks.text: Shintaro Uda built and studied the array in Japan in the 1920s and Hidetsugu Yagi published it in English, so both names stay. One element is driven: a half-wave dipole, often a folded dipole, whose input resistance of about 300 Ω suits a twin feeder. The other rods are parasitic: they sit on the boom but are not wired to the feed.

items: Driven element: 0.46λ to 0.48λ long, λ being the free-space wavelength at the design frequency.
Reflector: one rod behind the driven element, 0.50λ to 0.55λ long, 0.15λ to 0.25λ away.
Directors: rods in front, 0.40λ to 0.45λ long, each a little shorter than the one behind it, 0.15λ to 0.35λ apart.
Gain: about 7 dBi with one reflector and one director, 9 to 11 dBi with five elements, up to about 15 dBi for long booms; bandwidth 2 to 5 % of the design frequency.

blocks.text: Each parasitic rod carries a current induced by the driven element’s field and re-radiates. A rod longer than its resonant length (about λ/2) is inductive, a shorter one capacitive, so the rod length sets the phase of the induced current relative to the field that induces it; the spacing adds a path phase. With the reflector about 0.2λ behind, the two together make the reflector behave like the rear element of the cardioid pair (λ/4 apart, rear current leading by 90°): its wave cancels the driven element’s wave toward the back and adds toward the front. The directors are phased so that their waves stay in step with the wave moving forward along the boom, which makes the Yagi an end-fire array firing away from the reflector.
The phases come from lengths and spacings, so they are right only near one frequency. More directors raise the gain with diminishing returns: doubling the boom length adds roughly 2 to 3 dB.

A log-periodic antenna repeats its geometry at sizes in a fixed ratio, so its behaviour at frequency f repeats at f/τ, f/τ², and so on; if the steps are small, the properties hardly change in between. In the dipole version the dipoles shrink by τ from back to front, their tips lie on two straight lines from an apex, and the spacings shrink in step.
τ is the scale factor (less than 1, typically 0.8 to 0.95); L<sub>n</sub> is the length of dipole n counted from the longest; d<sub>n</sub> is the gap between dipoles n and n + 1.

blocks.where: σ is the spacing factor, typically 0.06 to 0.2; the half apex angle is α = tan⁻¹[(1 − τ)/(4σ)].

blocks.text: N is the number of dipoles, rounded up; B is the bandwidth ratio. The longest dipole is about λ/2 at f<sub>min</sub>: L<sub>1</sub> (m) = 150/f<sub>min</sub> (MHz).

All dipoles are fed from a two-wire line along the boom, with the connections crossed between neighbours, and the cable is connected at the short front end. At a given frequency only the few dipoles near half a wavelength carry large current: the active region. The crossed feed makes the active dipoles fire toward the short end. Behind the active region the longer dipoles carry little current; in front of it the short dipoles are too small to radiate. As the frequency rises the active region slides forward.

examples.question: Find the element lengths and spacings of a 3-element Yagi for a 500 MHz link using driven element 0.47λ, reflector 0.50λ at 0.25λ behind it, and director 0.45λ at 0.20λ in front. Give the boom length and the expected band.
steps: Driven element: 0.47 × 600 = 282 mm. Reflector: 0.50 × 600 = 300 mm. Director: 0.45 × 600 = 270 mm.
Reflector spacing: 0.25 × 600 = 150 mm behind; director spacing: 0.20 × 600 = 120 mm in front.
Boom from reflector to director: 150 + 120 = 270 mm, plus a little at each end for clamps.
A 3-element Yagi gives about 7 dBi (about 5 dBd). A 2 to 5 % band is 10 to 25 MHz wide, so it serves roughly 490 to 510 MHz.
examples.answer: Reflector 300 mm, driven element 282 mm, director 270 mm; spacings 150 mm and 120 mm on a 270 mm boom; about 7 dBi over roughly 490 to 510 MHz.

examples.question: An LPDA must cover 200 to 600 MHz with τ = 0.9, σ = 0.15 and a longest dipole of 750 mm. Find the number of dipoles, the shortest dipole, the half apex angle, the first spacing and the boom length. Which dipoles are active at 300 MHz?
steps: Check L<sub>1</sub>: λ/2 at 200 MHz is 1500/2 = 750 mm, as given.
Shortest dipole: L<sub>12</sub> = 750 × 0.9¹¹ = 750 × 0.3138 = 235.4 mm; it is half a wavelength at 150/0.2354 = 637 MHz, above 600 MHz, so the top of the band is covered.
First spacing: d<sub>1</sub> = 2σL<sub>1</sub> = 2 × 0.15 × 750 = 225 mm; then 202.5, 182.3, … down to d<sub>11</sub> = 78.5 mm.
Boom: (L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>12</sub>)/(2 tan α) = (750 − 235.4)/(2 × 0.1667) = 1544 mm, the same as the sum of the 11 spacings.
At 300 MHz, λ/2 = 500 mm, which lies between dipole 4 (546.8 mm) and dipole 5 (492.1 mm); the active region is dipoles 3 to 6.
examples.answer: 12 dipoles from 750 mm down to 235 mm, half apex angle 9.5°, first spacing 225 mm, boom about 1.54 m; at 300 MHz dipoles 4 and 5 do most of the radiating.

traps: Calling the Yagi wideband. Its band is a few per cent and more directors make it narrower, not wider.
Putting the LPDA’s longest dipole at the high frequency. The longest dipole works at f<sub>min</sub>; the active region moves to the short front end as f rises.
Swapping τ and σ. τ compares neighbouring lengths; σ compares a spacing with twice the length.
Mixing dBd and dBi. dBi = dBd + 2.15 dB; a “10 dB” Yagi in dBd is 12.15 dBi.
Feeding the LPDA at the long end. The cable goes to the short front end, and the beam leaves through it.

quiz.q: Is the Yagi reflector longer or shorter than the driven element, and where does it go?
quiz.a: Longer, about 0.50λ to 0.55λ, mounted 0.15λ to 0.25λ behind the driven element.

quiz.q: Define τ and σ of an LPDA.
quiz.a: τ = L<sub>n+1</sub>/L<sub>n</sub>, the ratio of neighbouring dipole lengths (0.8 to 0.95); σ = d<sub>n</sub>/(2L<sub>n</sub>), the spacing over twice the length (0.06 to 0.2).

quiz.q: What is the active region of an LPDA and why does it move?
quiz.a: The few dipoles near λ/2 long that carry most of the current. A higher frequency has a shorter λ/2, so the resonant group sits further toward the short end.

quiz.q: An LPDA must cover 100 to 1000 MHz with τ = 0.85. Find B and N.
An LPDA has a longest dipole of 600 mm, τ = 0.9 and 10 dipoles. Find the shortest dipole and the highest frequency it serves.
Why are neighbouring LPDA dipoles fed in antiphase? Use σ = 0.15 in the active region.
quiz.a: There d = 2σL ≈ 0.15λ, so βd = 54°. The feed wave runs from the front toward the back, so each dipole behind lags its front neighbour by 54° on the line plus 180° from the crossing. Toward the back, the front dipole’s wave lags 54° by path, so the two arrive 180° apart and cancel. Toward the front they arrive 2 × 54° + 180° = 288° apart, which is −72°, close to in phase, so they add. The beam leaves through the short end.

quiz.q: A Yagi cut for 400 MHz is used at 450 MHz. What happens?
quiz.a: Every rod is electrically longer than designed, so the induced-current phases are wrong: forward gain falls, the front-to-back ratio collapses, and the driven element is no longer matched, so the VSWR rises.

quiz.q: Why is a folded dipole often used as the Yagi driven element?
quiz.a: The parasitic rods pull the driven element’s resistance well below 73 Ω; a folded dipole steps it up about four times, closer to the feeder’s impedance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Yagis are now optimised with numerical electromagnetics codes such as NEC rather than by cut and try, and printed Yagis appear in millimetre-wave modules. Self-complementary log-periodic shapes and spirals extend the same idea to frequency-independent antennas that keep their impedance over a decade of bandwidth. Search for NEC antenna modelling, Carrel LPDA design and frequency-independent antennas.

figure.caption: The 12-dipole log-periodic array of the second worked example, drawn to scale: the dipoles shrink by τ = 0.9 from 750 mm to 235 mm, their tips lie on two lines from the apex 9.5° either side of the boom, and the boom is 1544 mm long. At 300 MHz dipoles 4 and 5, near half a wavelength, do the radiating; the cable connects at the short end and the beam leaves that way.
